notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the union area of two axis-aligned rectangles from their lower-left and upper-right coordinates.
Idea: Add the two rectangle areas and subtract the area of their intersection.
Technique and why it applies: The overlap width is max(0, min(C,G)-max(A,E)); the analogous vertical expression gives overlap height. Clamping each dimension to zero handles disjoint rectangles and edge-only contact.
Invariant: The returned value counts each covered point once by applying area(A)+area(B)-area(overlap).
Edge cases: Identical rectangles return one rectangle's area; disjoint rectangles subtract zero; touching edges have zero intersection area.
Complexity: A fixed number of arithmetic and min/max operations gives O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Both author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Evaluate a valid expression containing integers, plus, minus, parentheses, and spaces, including unary minus, without eval.
Idea: Scan the expression from right to left, collecting operands and operators, and evaluate operators as closing parentheses or the scan end is reached.
Technique and why it applies: Reversed scanning allows numbers to be assembled from right to left and makes operand pop order match the code's compute routine. Parentheses trigger reductions until the matching ')' operator is removed.
Invariant: operands stores parsed numbers and intermediate results; operators holds pending operators whose right-side values have already been read.
Edge cases: Whitespace is ignored. A unary minus is supported by the reversed operand/operator arrangement for valid expressions, while the input guarantees balanced parentheses and valid syntax.
Complexity: Each character and operator is processed a constant number of times, so time is O(n), with O(n) worst-case stack space. The author labels are consistent.

Task and constraints: Evaluate an expression with non-negative integers and +, -, *, /; division must truncate toward zero.
Idea: Parse each number, apply multiplication or division immediately to the latest stack value, and defer addition/subtraction until the final sum.
Technique and why it applies: Higher-precedence operations are collapsed as soon as the next operator is encountered. Addition pushes a positive term, subtraction pushes a negative term, and the final sum combines the terms.
Invariant: stack contains signed terms whose sum equals the processed expression, with multiplication/division already applied to each term.
Edge cases: Spaces do not trigger an operation. The final character forces the last number to be processed. Division uses int(stack.pop()/currentNumber), which truncates toward zero; valid input prevents division by zero.
Complexity: The parser scans n characters once, taking O(n) time; the stack can hold O(n) terms. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Convert a sorted unique integer array into the smallest list of consecutive ranges that covers exactly its elements.
Idea: Track the start and end indices of a run of consecutive values, then emit either a single number or a start->end string.
Technique and why it applies: The inner loop advances r while each value is exactly one greater than its predecessor. When a gap appears, the completed run is formatted and the next run begins.
Invariant: At emission time, nums[l:r] is a maximal consecutive run, and earlier emitted runs cover all preceding values without overlap.
Edge cases: An empty input returns an empty list. A singleton run is rendered without an arrow; negative values work because only differences of one are tested.
Complexity: Each index is advanced through once, so time is O(n) and output space is O(n). No author labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Summarize sorted unique integers into minimal consecutive ranges.
Idea: Group enumerated values by the difference between each value and its index; values in one group form a consecutive run.
Technique and why it applies: itertools.groupby groups equal value-index differences. Joining group values with arrows produces a chain, and the regular expression reduces the chain to its first and last values.
Invariant: Within each group, value-index is constant, which means every adjacent value differs by exactly one.
Edge cases: Empty input yields an empty list. A one-element group becomes a single-number string; negative and large integers are supported by repr.
Complexity: Grouping and formatting process n values, giving O(n) time and O(n) output/intermediate space. The author labels are broadly correct.

Task and constraints: Return the minimal sorted list of ranges representing all values in a sorted, unique integer array.
Idea: Maintain a start and end value for the current run and close the range whenever the next value is not consecutive.
Technique and why it applies: The loop checks nums[i] == end+1 to extend a run. Otherwise it formats the completed range, then initializes the next run from nums[i].
Invariant: start and end delimit the consecutive run currently being accumulated; every closed run is maximal and ordered after previous runs.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list. Single values are emitted without an arrow, and the loop runs one step beyond the last index to flush the final range.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time, and the returned list uses O(n) space. No author labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return all values appearing more than floor(n/3) times. There can be at most two such values.
Idea: Use two candidate values and counters with Boyer–Moore cancellation, then count each candidate exactly in a second pass.
Technique and why it applies: When neither candidate matches and both counters are positive, decrement both to cancel a triple of distinct values. The verification pass prevents unconfirmed candidates from being returned.
Invariant: After the first pass, any value occurring more than n/3 times must be among me1 and me2; the second pass establishes their actual frequencies.
Edge cases: One or two elements can yield one or two majorities. If neither candidate exceeds req, the function reaches the end without returning a list, producing None instead of the required empty list; this is a correctness issue.
Complexity: Two traversals take O(n) time and only a fixed number of counters are used, giving O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether an integer is a positive power of two, including 1; nonpositive values must be rejected.
Idea: Check positivity and test whether n has exactly one set bit.
Technique and why it applies: For positive n, -n in two's-complement arithmetic isolates the least significant set bit when combined with n; the expression n & ~-n is zero exactly when no other set bits remain.
Invariant: The bitwise condition is true only when the positive integer contains one set bit, matching 2^x.
Edge cases: n=1 passes; n=16 passes; n=3 fails. The n>0 guard rejects zero and negative numbers before the bit test.
Complexity: A fixed number of integer bitwise operations gives O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space under the usual fixed-width integer model. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return whether n is a power of two; the input may be negative or zero.
Idea: Require n to be positive and use n & (n-1) to check whether exactly one bit is set.
Technique and why it applies: Subtracting one from a positive power of two turns its sole set bit into zero and fills lower bits with ones, so the AND is zero. Any positive integer with multiple set bits leaves at least one bit set.
Invariant: The bit test is zero precisely for positive integers with one set bit.
Edge cases: 1 and 16 return True; 3, zero, and negative numbers return False because of the positivity guard or nonzero AND.
Complexity: The method uses a constant number of bitwise operations and variables, so O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space. The author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Count all occurrences of digit 1 in every integer from 0 through n, where n may be up to 10^9.
Idea: Examine each decimal place separately and count how often that place contributes a one.
Technique and why it applies: For place value pv, mul counts complete cycles of ten, rem captures the lower digits, and the current digit decides whether to add a full place or rem+1 additional occurrences.
Invariant: After processing a place, count includes all digit-one occurrences contributed by that decimal position across the range [0,n].
Edge cases: n=0 has one digit '0', so the method returns zero. The reversed string num is indexed consistently with place values because index i in the reversed string represents the original digit at 10^i.
Complexity: There are O(log n) decimal positions, with constant work per position; the string representation uses O(log n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Count the total number of digit ones in all non-negative integers not exceeding n.
Idea: Iterate through decimal place values 1, 10, 100, and so on, accumulating each position's contribution.
Technique and why it applies: The formula counts complete cycles using n//(10*base) and adds a partial cycle based on n%(10*base). DIGIT is one, so is_zero is zero and the generalized expression simplifies to the usual digit-one count.
Invariant: After each iteration, result contains the contributions from all processed decimal positions.
Edge cases: n=0 skips the loop and returns zero. The loop stops once base exceeds n, avoiding unnecessary higher positions.
Complexity: The number of iterations is O(log n), each with constant arithmetic, and auxiliary space is O(1). The author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Return the product of every array element except the element at the same index, without division.
Idea: Precompute prefix products and suffix products, multiply them at each index, and write the result into nums.
Technique and why it applies: pre[i] represents the product before index i; back[i] is intended to represent the product after index i. Their product excludes nums[i], including when zeros are present.
Invariant: For each i, pre[i]*back[i] equals the product of all values to the left and right of i. The suffix loop writes back[-1] at i=0, but that overwritten entry is not used for the returned positions.
Edge cases: Zero values are handled without division. The implementation mutates the input list and uses two additional length-n arrays.
Complexity: Prefix/suffix passes and output writes take O(n) time; pre and back require O(n) extra space, so this version does not meet the O(1)-extra-space follow-up. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Build an output where each position contains the product of all other values, without using division.
Idea: Store prefix products in the output list, then sweep backward while maintaining a running suffix product.
Technique and why it applies: left_product[i] first stores the product of elements before i. During the reverse pass, right_product accumulates elements after i and is multiplied into that prefix value.
Invariant: After the forward pass, left_product[i] equals the prefix product before i; after the reverse pass, each entry contains both sides' product excluding nums[i].
Edge cases: Zeros require no special handling, because no division is used. The empty-list guard returns an empty list, although the problem's constraints require at least two elements.
Complexity: The two passes are O(n) time. The left_product list is the returned output array, which the problem explicitly excludes from extra-space accounting; the suffix accumulator is constant-sized, so O(1) extra space is valid. The author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum of every sliding window of size k, with 1 <= k <= len(nums).
Idea: Maintain a max-heap of negative values paired with their indices, adding each incoming value and removing expired heap tops.
Technique and why it applies: Negating values lets Python's min-heap act as a max-heap. Stored indices identify entries that are no longer inside the current window.
Invariant: Before each answer is appended, the heap top is the largest value among entries whose indices remain in the current window.
Edge cases: k=1 returns each value; k=len(nums) returns one maximum. The snippet references heapq without importing it, so it raises NameError unless the module is imported elsewhere.
Complexity: Each insertion/removal costs O(log n), so time is O(n log n); stale entries not at the top remain in the heap, allowing O(n) heap space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute the maximum for every contiguous window of length k.
Idea: Keep indices in a deque ordered so their corresponding values decrease from front to back.
Technique and why it applies: Expired indices leave the front; values no larger than the new value leave the back because they cannot become a future maximum while the new value remains in the window.
Invariant: The deque contains candidate indices in decreasing value order, and its front is the maximum index for the current window.
Edge cases: k=1 appends every element as its own window maximum; k=len(nums) produces one answer. Equal values are removed from the back in favor of the newer index.
Complexity: Each index is appended once and removed at most once, giving O(n) time and O(k) deque space. No author labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Search for target in a matrix whose rows and columns are sorted in ascending order.
Idea: Visit every cell and remember whether any cell equals target.
Technique and why it applies: The nested loops compare each matrix value with target. Although the sorted properties could support pruning, this implementation does not use them and does not stop after finding a match.
Invariant: found is True once any inspected cell matches target and remains True for the rest of the scan.
Edge cases: If target is absent, the full matrix is scanned and False is returned. If present, scanning still continues after found becomes True. The statement guarantees a nonempty matrix.
Complexity: Every one of the m*n cells is visited, so time is O(mn); only a Boolean is stored, giving O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether target occurs in a matrix sorted by rows and columns.
Idea: Start at the top-right corner and eliminate one row or column on each comparison.
Technique and why it applies: If the current value is too large, every value below it in that column is at least as large, so move left. If too small, every value to its left in the row is no larger, so move down.
Invariant: The remaining search region contains target if it has not already been found; each comparison safely discards one row or column.
Edge cases: Empty row/column checks return False, though the problem guarantees nonempty dimensions. A match returns immediately.
Complexity: At most m downward and n leftward moves occur, giving O(m+n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. The author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Return all results obtainable by inserting parentheses into an expression of numbers and +, -, * operators.
Idea: Split at every operator, recursively compute the left and right subexpressions, and combine every pair of results.
Technique and why it applies: Each possible final operation corresponds to one split point; Cartesian combinations of left and right results enumerate the parenthesizations. The intended memo dictionary m is not actually passed into recursive calls, which call diffWaysToCompute anew, so memoization is ineffective.
Invariant: For each split, ret accumulates every combination of a valid left result and right result using the split operator.
Edge cases: A digits-only substring returns its integer. The code calls eval on generated expressions even though the prompt explicitly prohibits eval; this violates the task requirement.
Complexity: Because recursive calls redo overlapping subproblems, runtime can grow exponentially with operator count, plus output combinations; recursion and intermediate result lists consume additional space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Enumerate all possible results from different parenthesizations of an expression containing integers and +, -, *.
Idea: Memoize results for substring intervals and recursively try every operator as the final split.
Technique and why it applies: Each operator divides an interval into left and right subexpressions; combining their result lists with the corresponding operator enumerates all valid parenthesizations. The lookup table avoids recomputing cached intervals.
Invariant: lookup[left][right] stores all results for input[left:right] once that interval has been evaluated.
Edge cases: An interval with no operator is parsed as one integer. The truthiness check treats a cached empty list as a cache miss, but valid expression intervals should have at least one result.
Complexity: There are O(n²) possible intervals, but combining result lists can be exponential in operator count because the output itself may be large. The lookup table uses O(n²) references plus storage for intermediate result lists. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether t is an anagram of s, meaning both strings contain the same characters with the same frequencies. The stated alphabet is lowercase English letters.
Idea: Count each character in both strings and compare the two frequency mappings.
Technique and why it applies: Counter aggregates multiplicities, so equality means every character appears equally often in both strings; ordering does not matter.
Invariant: Each counter maps a character to its number of occurrences, and equality checks all represented frequencies.
Edge cases: Different lengths or differing letter counts yield False; rearranged strings with matching counts yield True. The snippet references Counter without importing it, so it raises NameError unless Counter is available in the surrounding environment.
Complexity: Counting takes O(|s|+|t|) time. With the fixed lowercase alphabet, each counter has at most 26 keys, so auxiliary space is O(1) under that constraint; for arbitrary Unicode it scales with distinct characters. No labels were supplied.
